title: Electronegativity trends in the periodic table
body: Electronegativity increases left to right across a period and decreases down a group, which can be explained with electronic structure, the shell model, and Coulomb's law.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.1 "increase going from left to right across a period and decrease going down a group"

title: Nonpolar covalent bond
body: A nonpolar covalent bond is formed when valence electrons are shared between atoms of similar electronegativity (e.g., C–H is effectively nonpolar).
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.2 "Valence electrons shared between atoms of similar electronegativity constitute a nonpolar covalent bond"

title: Polar covalent bond
body: A polar covalent bond is formed when valence electrons are shared between atoms of unequal electronegativity.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.3 "Valence electrons shared between atoms of unequal electronegativity constitute a polar covalent bond"

title: Direction and size of a bond dipole
body: In a polar bond the more electronegative atom takes the partial negative charge, and in single bonds a greater electronegativity difference gives a greater bond dipole.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.3.i–ii "greater differences in electronegativity lead to greater bond dipoles"

title: Classifying a bond as ionic or covalent
body: Metal–nonmetal bonds are generally ionic and nonmetal–nonmetal bonds are generally covalent, but electronegativity difference alone does not decide it, and the compound's properties are the best way to characterize the bonding.
caution: All polar bonds have some ionic character, so ionic and covalent bonding form a continuum rather than two distinct categories.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.4 "Examination of the properties of a compound is the best way to characterize the type of bonding"; 2.1.A.3.iii

title: Delocalized valence electrons (metallic solid)
body: In a metallic solid, the valence electrons from the metal atoms are delocalized and not associated with any individual atom.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.5 "delocalized and not associated with any individual atom"

title: Potential energy vs. internuclear distance graph
body: A graph of potential energy versus the distance between atoms shows the equilibrium bond length and the bond energy.

items.label: x-axis: internuclear distance
items.meaning: Distance between the nuclei of the two atoms, with scale and units.

items.label: y-axis: potential energy
items.meaning: Potential energy of the pair of atoms, with scale and units.

items.label: Equilibrium bond length
items.meaning: The separation between atoms at which the potential energy is lowest.

items.label: Bond energy
items.meaning: The energy required to separate the atoms.

ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 "equilibrium bond length (the separation between atoms at which the potential energy is lowest) and the bond energy"

title: Bond order, bond length, and bond energy
body: Covalent bond length depends on the size of the atoms' cores and on bond order, and bonds of higher order (single, double, triple) are shorter and have larger bond energies.
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.2 "Bonds with a higher order are shorter and have larger bond energies"

title: Coulomb's law and cation–anion interaction strength
body: Larger ion charges give stronger interactions, and smaller ions (shorter distance between the ion centers) give stronger interactions.

items.label: Larger charges
items.meaning: Interaction strength is proportional to the charge on each ion, so stronger.

items.label: Smaller ions
items.meaning: Interaction strength increases as the distance between nuclei decreases, so stronger.

ced_evidence: 2.2.A.3.i–ii "larger charges lead to stronger interactions"; "smaller ions lead to stronger interactions"

title: Particulate model of an ionic solid
body: Cations and anions sit in a systematic, periodic 3-D array that maximizes attractive forces and minimizes repulsive forces among the ions.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.1 "systematic, periodic 3-D array that maximizes the attractive forces among cations and anions while minimizing the repulsive forces"

title: Sea-of-electrons model of metallic bonding
body: A metallic solid is drawn as an array of positive metal ions surrounded by delocalized valence electrons.

items.label: Positive metal ions
items.meaning: Cores of the metal atoms arranged in an array.

items.label: Delocalized valence electrons
items.meaning: The "sea of electrons" surrounding the ions, not tied to any one atom.

ced_evidence: 2.4.A.1 "array of positive metal ions surrounded by delocalized valence electrons (i.e., a 'sea of electrons')"

title: Interstitial alloy
body: An interstitial alloy forms between atoms of significantly different radii, with the smaller atoms filling the interstitial spaces between the larger atoms (e.g., carbon in the interstices of iron in steel).
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.2 "smaller atoms fill the interstitial spaces between the larger atoms"

title: Substitutional alloy
body: A substitutional alloy forms between atoms of comparable radius, with one atom substituting for the other in the lattice (e.g., zinc substituting for copper in certain brasses).
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.3 "atoms of comparable radius, where one atom substitutes for the other in the lattice"

title: Formal charge of an atom in a Lewis diagram
body: \text{FC} = V - N_{\text{nonbonding}} - \tfrac{1}{2}N_{\text{bonding}}
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.2 "The octet rule and formal charge can be used as criteria"

title: Resonance for equivalent Lewis structures
body: When more than one equivalent Lewis structure can be drawn, resonance must be included as a refinement to give qualitatively accurate predictions of molecular structure and properties.
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.1 "resonance must be included as a refinement to the Lewis structure"

title: Choosing among nonequivalent Lewis diagrams
body: The octet rule and formal charge are the criteria used to decide which valid Lewis diagram is the best model for predicting molecular structure and properties.
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.2 "The octet rule and formal charge can be used as criteria for determining which of several possible valid Lewis diagrams provides the best model"

title: Limitation of the Lewis model
body: The Lewis structure model has limitations, particularly for species with an odd number of valence electrons.
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.3 "particularly in cases with an odd number of valence electrons"

title: VSEPR theory
body: VSEPR theory uses the Coulombic repulsion between electrons to predict the arrangement of electron pairs around a central atom.
caution: VSEPR must be used together with the Lewis diagram to predict molecular geometry, bond angles, and dipole moment.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.1 "Coulombic repulsion between electrons as a basis for predicting the arrangement of electron pairs"

title: Molecular geometries named in the CED
body: The molecular geometries students must predict from Lewis diagrams and VSEPR, in CED order.

items.label: Linear
items.meaning: 2 electron domains, no lone pairs on the central atom

items.label: Bent
items.meaning: Central atom with lone pairs (3 domains with 1 lone pair, or 4 domains with 2 lone pairs)

caution: Molecular geometry names the arrangement of atoms and is not the same as a bond angle. Give the geometry name, not just an angle such as 109.5°.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.2.i "linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent, trigonal bipyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, octahedral, square pyramidal, square planar"

title: Hybridization and ideal bond angles
body: The ideal bond angle for each hybridization label (sp, sp², sp³).
caution: To assign hybridization, count regions of electron density around the central atom. A double bond is one region, so a carbon in C=O with three regions is sp², not sp³. Answer with the hybridization label, not a geometry or angle.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.3 "sp hybridized, its ideal bond angles are 180°; for sp2 ... 120°; and for sp3 ... 109.5°"

title: Sigma and pi bonds
body: Bond formation involves orbital overlap, and multiple bonds contain both sigma and pi bonds; sigma overlap is stronger, so sigma bonds have greater bond energy than pi bonds, and a pi bond prevents rotation about the bond and leads to geometric isomers.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.4 "sigma bonds having greater bond energy than pi bonds. The presence of a pi bond also prevents the rotation of the bond and leads to geometric isomers"
